about: Which letter-sound units a word may use at each stage of the Word Sounds word picker, with the document that places each group of units there. Each stage adds to the stages before it. "standard" means a document opened on the date above names that kind of unit at that grade or year; "common practice" means no opened document does, and the placement follows classroom convention (the sources then show what the documents do say). After editing: node dev-tools/build_word_sounds_wordlist.cjs
unitNotation: A unit is letters>sound as word_sounds_core.js lines them up (sh>sh, x>k+s). "/pattern" marks a long vowel written with one letter: /silent_e (make), /open_syllable (go, ba-by), /single_letter (find, old), /y_as_vowel (my, happy). "*" means every unit.
limitsNotation: maxSyllables and maxSounds: 0 means no limit; syllables are counted as vowel sounds in the sound dictionary. clusters: two consonant sounds side by side are allowed. longVowelsInLongerWords: false means a word of two or more syllables may not hold a long vowel sound. avoidFinal: sounds (or the letter x) a word may not end with.

frameworks.note: The standards say what a child should be able to do by the END of each grade. They do not split a grade into parts and do not give an order inside a grade: the early and late halves here, and the order inside each row, are common practice, not a standard. The order of the halves follows the order the IES practice guide suggests (single letters, then blends and consonant digraphs, then silent e, then vowel teams).

noteSources.quote: Present consonants and short vowel sounds represented by single letters first [...] The panel recommends next introducing consonant blends (e.g., fl, sm, st) and common two-letter consonant digraphs (e.g., sh, th, ch). [...] Then teach long vowels with silent e, and finally two-letter vowel teams (vowel digraphs, e.g., ea and ou).

stages.label: Kindergarten, first part: three-sound words, one letter for each sound, short vowels (cat, sun, hop)

limits.why: One syllable, three sounds at most, no two consonant sounds side by side, and no word that ends in /l/, /r/ or the letter x: the kindergarten standard names three-sound consonant-vowel-consonant words and sets those endings aside. It is a standard about hearing sounds; it is used for the whole stage because the packet activities are sound activities. Consonant blends are named in grade 1 (RF.1.2.b).

Add or substitute individual sounds (phonemes) in simple, one-syllable words to make new words.
Orally produce single-syllable words by blending sounds (phonemes), including consonant blends.

limits.why: The appendix sets no length. Its Year 2 example words run to three syllables (enjoyment, happiness, hospital), so three is used.

groups.notSaid: The appendix teaches these as exception words, word by word, not as a pattern.

differencesInShort: England's statutory appendix teaches most patterns one to two years earlier than the Common Core places them: consonant digraphs and blends in Reception (ages 4 to 5) against grade 1; final e, nearly all vowel digraphs and r-controlled vowels in Year 1 (ages 5 to 6) against grade 1 and grade 2; -tion in Year 2 (ages 6 to 7) against grade 3. The Common Core standards do not name r-controlled vowels, doubled final letters, soft c and g, -dge, -tch, silent letters or consonant + le at any grade.

claims.may: The order of spelling patterns follows the grade placements in the Common Core Reading Foundational Skills standards. Where the standards do not place a pattern, it follows common classroom practice, and the stage table shows which is which.
mayAlso: How familiar a word is comes from CYP-LEX, a published count of the words in 400 books popular with children aged 7 to 9 in the United Kingdom (Korochkina, Marelli, Brysbaert & Rastle, 2024; CC BY 4.0), together with the app's own word lists.
An England option follows the statutory requirements of the National Curriculum spelling appendix for Years 1 and 2.
The halves of kindergarten and grade 1 are in the order the IES practice guide (2016) suggests for teaching letter-sound patterns.
mustNot: That the tool is aligned to, approved by or endorsed by the Common Core, the NGA Center, CCSSO, the Department for Education, IES or the What Works Clearinghouse.
That it follows or is aligned to any reading programme or method (for example UFLI, Orton-Gillingham, Fundations, Letters and Sounds) or to "the science of reading".
That the order is research-based, evidence-based or proven: the documents place skills by grade and suggest an order; nobody tested this table.
That the standards split kindergarten or grade 1 into early and late parts, or give an order inside a grade: those are this tool's.
That a word is at grade level, levelled, normed, benchmarked or decodable for a particular child.
That the familiarity data shows which words kindergarten or grade 1 children know: it counts British books for ages 7 to 9.
That every word offered is suitable: the blocklist is a first pass that needs human review.
That r-controlled vowels, doubled final letters, soft c and g, -dge, -tch, silent letters or consonant + le are placed by the Common Core standards: they are not named there.
